item.title: Apotex reports Q2 profit, raises guidance for revenue growth for the year
item.description: Apotex Health Corp. raised its guidance for its full year as it reported a second-quarter profit of $100.8 million, up from $82.9 million a year earlier.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Apotex Health Corp. raised its guidance for its full year as it reported a second-quarter profit of $100.8 million, up from $82.9 million a year earlier. The drug company says the profit amounted to 41 cents per diluted share for the quarter compared with 43 cents per diluted share a year ago when it had fewer shares outstanding. Revenue totalled $852.9 million for the quarter, up from $843.5 million in the same quarter last year. On an adjusted basis, Apotex says it earned 57 cents per diluted share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted profit of 61 cents per diluted share a year earlier. In its updated outlook, it says it now expects full-year revenue growth of nine to 10 per cent, up from earlier expectations for upper mid-single digit growth of seven to eight per cent. Apotex also says it now expects its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization margin to come in at about 31 per cent, up from earlier guidance for about 30 per cent. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

item.title: Investors worry the AI trade might lose Nvidia’s largesse after Huang
item.description: As chip giant Nvidia’s chief Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday, investors’ biggest fears were as much about the future of the multitrillion-dollar company as its ability and willingness to ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: SINGAPORE -- As chip giant Nvidia’s chief Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday, investors’ biggest fears were as much about the future of the multitrillion-dollar company as its ability and willingness to continue bankrolling the AI boom. Huang’s exit is yet another pressure point on the global markets’ most crowded trade and came after the board of the world’s dominant chipmaker, at the cutting edge of computing, met late on Wednesday to decide the longtime CEO’s fate after reports of his two extramarital affairs. The company said Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor. Traders’ first reaction was to punish Nvidia shares and those of its customers, including data-centre firms CoreWeave and Naver, while pushing shares of chipmaking rivals Broadcom and AMD higher. Shares in China’s leading makers of graphics processing units (GPUs) surged, as the leadership upheaval at Nvidia boosted expectations that local chip suppliers could win greater market share. Moore Threads, MetaX and Cambricon all jumped nearly 10 per cent. Nvidia shares pared premarket losses but were still down nearly five per cent at 1600 GMT. The worry in the market is that the stakes are far higher and that if Nvidia — under a different leader — backs away from a strategy of financing data centers, then the AI boom itself loses momentum. “Nvidia has been called the ‘Bank of AI.’ They’ll sell you the chips and loan you the money. If they have to take a step back because of what’s going on, will that cut off funding to smaller companies that need it? That’s an open question,” said Joe Saluzzi, partner and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading in Chatham, New Jersey. Nvidia has been the banner stock of the AI revolution, with its chip technology ahead of rivals and enormous sales driving the share price up some 900 per cent over the four years since the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT ushered in the AI era. But Nvidia has also become a torchbearer and financier, anticipating demand for ever more powerful chips while sinking billions of dollars into funding its own customers via a mix of equity investments and other promises. “Nvidia’s credit support is what makes much of this debt finance-able across the AI hyperscaler deal front,” said Christopher Brown, senior vice president, investments, at Synovus Securities. “Lenders will ask what happens to that support if Nvidia’s leadership or regulatory standing is impaired, and Nvidia’s own willingness to extend more guarantees may be constrained.” Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into Huang following reports he had an extramarital affair with a businesswoman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy. A subsequent report about another affair came out ahead of Wednesday’s board meeting. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, said Nvidia’s revenue would not suddenly plunge after Huang’s exit and, therefore, the bigger concern was about the future, given Huang was the person with the vision for computing. “Replacing that strategic vision ... is an enormous challenge,” he said. Nvidia sinks and takes some, but not all, along Huang’s departure leaves a vacuum at the top of the roughly US$4 trillion chipmaker that he co-founded and built over more than three decades to become the top supplier of chips and the nexus of the U.S.-China technology rivalry. Chipmakers in Asia, whose stocks have soared with Nvidia and the AI spending boom, but lately sagged on worries about funding costs and the demand outlook, slipped. Nvidia listed $164.5 billion in financial commitments in its most recent earnings report, with an obligation capped at $105 billion on an OpenAI data centre in Ohio and lease and other capacity guarantees topping $50 billion. In August, it said it had partnered with six major financial institutions including Apollo, BlackRock and Blackstone to launch compute financing platforms aimed at raising over $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure. Huang said then the company had the option to backstop up to $125 billion, or 25 per cent of the potential deals. “The interlocking deals that Nvidia has with so much of the industry raises the question into whether that created more stability or more fragility,” said Steve Sosnick, chief market analyst at Interactive Brokers in Connecticut. Nvidia is also one of the investors in Claude chatbot creator Anthropic’s initial public offering. The listing this month is set to serve as a test of investor appetite for all things AI. Shares in Nvidia-backed data-centre operator CoreWeave, which surged on Wednesday on upbeat earnings, fell more than six per cent. Shares in South Korea’s Naver, in which Nvidia took a $1 billion stake by financing a data-center expansion, also dropped six per cent. To be sure, investors said, the quality of Nvidia’s products is not likely to change, and change at the top won’t quickly hit demand. “Nvidia’s core asset is its advanced GPUs, which still have no real substitute in the market,” said Anna Wu, founder of Floodlines Research. “The AI trade rests on that demand, not on one individual.” But when the company reports earnings next week, the focus will inevitably be on leadership, strategy and whether a sales outlook formed under Huang still holds up under a successor. (Reporting by Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Tom Westbrook in Sydney, Prathik Jayaprakash, Anhata Rooprai, Lakshmi Tharuniyaa, Johann Cherian in Bengaluru and Li Gu in Shanghai; Editing by Thomas Derpinghaus, Vidya Ranganathan, Mark Potter and Emelia Sithole-Matarise)

item.title: World shares are mixed as Nvidia's troubles weigh on AI stocks
item.description: World shares were mixed on Thursday as concerns over leadership at chipmaker Nvidia weighed on artificial intelligence-related stocks.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market has erased its early losses on Thursday after absorbing big swings for Nvidia’s stock and oil prices. The moves suggest Wall Street sees limited fallout for the artificial intelligence industry, which carries immense influence on the market, following the sudden fall for one of its biggest evangelists. After dropping nearly one per cent at the start of trading, the S&P 500 quickly erased all of the loss and turned 0.3 per cent higher. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 195 points, or 0.4 per cent, as of 11:30 a.m. Eastern time, while the Nasdaq composite was up 0.3 per cent after eliminating its early drop of 1.6 per cent. At the centre of the swings was Nvidia’s stock. It plunged 14 per cent at the start of trading following the resignation of Jensen Huang, its CEO, co-founder and face of the brand. The chip company’s stock has been sinking since its board announced an investigation into Huang for a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese government agent. It’s a stunning fall for Huang and for Nvidia, which had become Wall Street’s most valuable and influential stock because of its central role in the AI boom. Its stock price set a record last month after soaring an astounding 1,722 per cent in four years. That compares with the already healthy gain of nearly 109 per cent for the overall S&P 500 over the same time. But Nvidia’s price dropped 27 per cent from then through Wednesday on worries about whether Huang would remain as CEO and how Nvidia would navigate a future without him. Nvidia’s board answered the first question Thursday morning, when it said Huang resigned, and it named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as its interim CEO. The second question remains to be determined. And it looms over the entire market because Nvidia and the broader AI industry have been the main reasons the U.S. stock market has set so many records in recent years. Nvidia, to be sure, is still selling AI chips at a quick rate regardless of who stands on a stage and talks them up, and analysts said it remains the industry’s leader. That helped Nvidia quickly halve its early loss from Thursday, and its stock was most recently down 4.8 per cent. That paring helped the broader market to recover. Outside of Nvidia, other stocks across the AI industry swung in the uncertainty. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, fell 4.5 per cent. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers that’s been getting gobbled up in the AI frenzy, sank 2.5 per cent. But Broadcom rose 6.7 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices added 6.5 per cent on hopes the rival chip companies will gain a competitive advantage. Those two gains nearly offset the drop for Nvidia, which was the single heaviest weight on the S&P 500. That suggests investors see the AI business expanding to other players rather than depending on Nvidia. Demonstrating how much uncertainty was washing through the market was GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres. It flipped from an early loss of 3 per cent to a gain of 2.9 per cent. Also helping to support the U.S. market were gains for companies in the oil and gas industry. Marathon Petroleum climbed 2.6 per cent, and ExxonMobil added 1.2 per cent. They benefited from a rise in oil prices after U.S. President Donald Trump said he’s no longer interested in a deal with Iran to end their war. Instead of that, Trump said he asked his vice president to investigate U.S. cities and states run by Democrats. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump said. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil suddenly went from about US$92 to more than US$94 following Trump’s posting, before it later eased back. It was most recently at US$93.77, up 1.1 per cent. It’s been veering sharply since the United States and Israel began the war with Iran in late February, bouncing between roughly US$70 and US$150. Higher oil prices push up worries about inflation, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5.08 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Tuesday. Trading in the bond market had been closed Wednesday for Veterans Day. Higher yields make borrowing money more expensive for everyone, from the U.S. government to companies building AI data centres to regular people buying houses. High mortgage rates helped send sales of previously occupied U.S. homes in October to their slowest pace in more than 16 years. The housing industry has been slowing the U.S. economy but not upending it. A separate report on Thursday said that slightly more U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, but the number remains relatively low compared with history. In stock markets abroad, indexes ticked higher in Europe following a weaker finish in Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writer Yuri Kageyama contributed to this report.

item.title: Stan Wong’s Top Picks for Nov. 12, 2026
item.description: The outlook for global equities remains constructive despite recent market volatility. The U.S. economy has maintained steady growth, and corporate earnings continue to grow. Persistent inflation and ...
item.content:encoded:
Stan Wong, Portfolio Manager, Scotia Wealth Management Focus: North American Large Caps & ETFs

Top Picks: Alphabet , iShares Semiconductor ETF , Vanguard Industrials ETF MARKET OUTLOOK: The outlook for global equities remains constructive despite recent market volatility. The U.S. economy has maintained steady growth, and corporate earnings continue to grow. Persistent inflation and elevated bond yields remain risks, especially for stocks whose valuations leave little room for earnings disappointments. Technology has seen some of the sharpest swings. In the recent market decline, the Nasdaq-100 fell about 15 per cent from peak to trough, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 40 per cent. The selling pressure extended to companies supplying power and equipment for data centers as investors reassessed the regulatory outlook following the U.S. midterm elections. The selloff may also have been intensified by hedge funds exiting crowded and, in some cases, leveraged positions tied to artificial intelligence. The market reaction appears to have overstated the long-term risk to AI investment. Permitting delays and power constraints remain legitimate near-term challenges, as they can raise costs and postpone projects. However, global demand for computing capacity continues to grow, several states within the U.S. are competing to attract data center projects, and strategic competition with China gives the U.S. another reason to keep building. For investors, the question is whether share prices have fallen further than the earnings outlook warrants. Order backlogs, margins and cash flow can help gauge whether project delays are starting to weigh on earnings prospects. At The Stan Wong Group, we continue to favour high-quality large-cap businesses with resilient cash flows, durable competitive advantages and strong growth prospects. We remain disciplined about what we pay for that growth. As always, investment decisions should be made within the context of each investor’s broader total wealth plan. How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google Market-moving news, fast:  Get the BNN Bloomberg App now Sign up for the Market Call Top Picks newsletter at  bnnbloomberg.ca/newsletters TOP PICKS: Stan Wong’s Top Picks: Alphabet, iShares Semiconductor ETF & Vanguard Industrials ETF Stan Wong, portfolio manager at Scotia Wealth Management, shares his top stock picks to watch in the market.

Alphabet (GOOGL NASD) Alphabet’s recent drawdown of more than 30 per cent has created an unusual opportunity to invest in one of the world’s highest-quality technology companies at a notably lower valuation. The shares now trade at approximately 18 times forward earnings, below their 10-year average of about 20.7 times. Alphabet is much more than a search company. Its businesses span Search, YouTube, Google Cloud, subscriptions and Waymo, giving it several powerful ways to monetize artificial intelligence. The latest results showed that AI is strengthening rather than disrupting the core business. Revenue increased 25 per cent to US$127.6 billion, while Search revenue grew 12 per cent and query growth reached its fastest pace in five years. Gemini has reached one billion users, demonstrating enormous scale in generative AI. Google Cloud is becoming a much larger earnings engine. Revenue more than doubled to US$30.7 billion, while operating income more than tripled to US$11.1 billion. Cloud backlog reached US$561 billion, with more than half expected to become revenue within two years, providing strong visibility into future growth. Meeting that demand requires substantial investment. Alphabet expects 2026 capital expenditures of US$195 billion to US$205 billion, primarily for AI and cloud infrastructure. This is pressuring near-term free cash flow, but approximately US$265 billion in cash and marketable securities gives Alphabet considerable capacity to fund the buildout. When the shares last crossed the 30 per cent drawdown threshold in September 2022, they gained 36.8 per cent over the following 12 months. Technically, the shares appear to be stabilizing, and a recovery toward the 200-day moving average would confirm improving momentum. iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX NASD) The iShares Semiconductor ETF provides diversified exposure to 30 leading semiconductor companies and seeks to track the investment results of the NYSE Semiconductor Index. Major holdings include AMD, Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron and Intel. Its management fee is 0.33 per cent. Semiconductors are the essential building blocks of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, smartphones, automobiles, industrial automation and defence. AI-driven demand is broadening beyond graphics processors into memory, networking chips, power-management semiconductors and advanced packaging. Global AI-server revenue is projected to increase 64 per cent in 2026 to US$462 billion, with AI servers expected to represent 77 per cent of total server revenue. SOXX provides exposure across this expanding value chain without requiring investors to identify one eventual winner. The recent selloff has dramatically improved valuations. The NYSE Semiconductor Index currently trades at approximately 15 times forward earnings, nearly half the peak multiple reached during 2025 and back to levels last seen in 2022. SOXX recently experienced a drawdown of 40 per cent. Bloomberg analysis of previous SOXX drawdowns of at least 40 per cent over the past 25 years shows an average 12-month forward return of 25.3 per cent, with positive returns 75 per cent of the time. While history does not guarantee the same result, severe semiconductor corrections have often created attractive long-term buying opportunities. From a technical perspective, the correction has reset momentum and created a more attractive entry point. SOXX has begun to stabilize and is working back toward its 200-day moving average. A recovery above that level would provide further confirmation of improving momentum. Compelling valuations and a powerful growth outlook reinforce the long-term opportunity. Vanguard Industrials ETF (VIS NYSE) The Vanguard Industrials ETF provides exposure to nearly 400 U.S. industrial companies for a low expense ratio of 0.09 per cent. Major holdings include Caterpillar, GE Aerospace, RTX, Eaton and Deere. This diversified portfolio captures several important long-term investment themes. The U.S. industrial cycle is gaining momentum. Core capital-goods orders increased 14.1 per cent year over year, signalling stronger business investment. Manufacturing reshoring, infrastructure renewal, aerospace and defence spending, electrification and grid modernization are creating sustained demand for machinery, transportation, engineering and electrical equipment. Artificial intelligence provides another powerful growth engine. Data center construction spending is forecast to increase 33 per cent in 2026 and a further 25 per cent in 2027. The benefits extend beyond technology companies because these facilities require electrical equipment, cooling systems, automation, construction machinery and reliable power. Many VIS holdings provide the physical infrastructure required to build and operate the AI economy. The ETF combines established industrial leaders with companies positioned at the core of the power and data center buildout, reducing reliance on any one company or theme. It also provides exposure to a recovery in traditional capital spending beyond AI. From a technical perspective, VIS recently experienced a drawdown of almost 15 per cent following a strong multi-year advance. The pullback has improved the risk-reward profile, and the ETF is now recovering toward its 200-day moving average. A sustained move above that level would strengthen the technical outlook. Improving capital spending, durable secular growth drivers and broad diversification reinforce our positive view.
